arXiv:2209.06240v1 [astro-ph.IM] 13 Sep 2022

Multi-group Radiation Magneto-hydrodynamics based on Discrete Ordinates including Compton Scattering

Yan-Fei Jiang(姜燕飞) Affiliation: Center for Computational Astrophysics,
Flatiron Institute,
New York, NY 10010, USA
Abstract

We present a formulation and numerical algorithm to extend the scheme for grey radiation magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD) developed by [32] to include the frequency dependence via the multi-group approach. The entire frequency space can be divided into arbitrary number of groups in the lab frame, and we follow the time dependent evolution of frequency integrated specific intensities along discrete rays inside each group. Spatial transport of photons is done in the lab frame while all the coupling terms are solved in the fluid rest frame. Lorentz transformation is used to connect different frames. Radiation transport equation is solved fully implicitly in time while the MHD equations are evolved explicitly so that time step is not limited by the speed of light. A finite volume approach is used for transport in both spatial and frequency spaces to conserve radiation energy density and momentum. The algorithm includes photon absorption, electron scattering as well as Compton scattering, which is calculated by solving the Kompaneets equation. The algorithm is accurate for a wide range of optical depth conditions and can handle both radiation pressure and gas pressure dominated flows. It works for both Cartesian and curvilinear coordinate systems with adaptive mesh refinement. We provide a variety of test problems including radiating sphere, shadow test, absorption of a moving gas, Bondi type flows as well as a collection of test problems for thermal and bulk Compton scattering. We also discuss examples where frequency dependence can make a big difference compared with the grey approach.

Keywords: 
Computational methods (1965); Astrophysical fluid dynamics(101); Radiative transfer (1335); Radiative transfer simulations(1967)

I Introduction

Radiation magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) simulations play an important role for theoretical studies of many astrophysical problems. They can be used to determine thermal properties of the system with the dynamical evolution together, which can be directly connected to many observables such as lightcurves and spectra. In many cases, momentum and energy exchanges between photons and plasma provide the dominant pressure as well as heating and cooling source and radiation transport (RT) is essential in the simulations [see the review 77, and references therein]. Properties of photons are described by the fundamental quantity, specific intensity, which can vary with time, space, photon propagation direction, frequency as well as polarization in general. However, different levels of approximations are typically adopted to simplify the calculation. One simplification is to take the moments of specific intensities and make certain assumptions to close the moment equations such as Flux-limited diffusion (FLD) [41, 80, 39, 82, 90, 92, 40, e.g.,], the M1 approach [15, 55, 22, 69, 65, 43, 68, 1], or using variable Eddington tensors as obtained by solving another set of time-independent transport equation based on short characteristics [71, 29, 34, 12, 3, 44]. Another important simplification is that the evolved radiation field is typically integrated over the frequency space and different types of averaged opacities are adopted in the calculation.

In cases when radiation spectrum cannot be described by a simple formula such as blackbody, or the traditional averaged opacities (such as Rosseland mean and Planck mean) cannot be used, frequency dependence also needs to be included in RT calculations. For example, UV and infrared photons are typically emitted by different sources and they can have very different interactions with gas and dust particles. Near the photosphere where diffusion assumption cannot apply, even under the approximation of local thermal equilibrium (LTE), Rosseland mean opacities may not describe the momentum exchange between radiation and gas correctly. This is also the region where radiation spectrum can differ from blackbody significantly and frequency dependent RT is needed. There are several ways to include the frequency dependence of photons in RT calculations. The first straight forward approach is to solve the RT equation at discrete frequencies and the full spectrum is sampled with a certain number of frequency points [16]. This approach is typically taken by Monte Carlo RT calculations (see the recent review by Noebauer & Sim 50 and references therein) and many ray-tracing type RT solvers that are based on short or long characteristics [45, 28, 12, 20, 88, see, e.g.,]. Because radiation MHD calculations are typically much more expensive than MHD simulations and the cost will increase at least linearly with the number of frequency points, another commonly used approach to include the frequency dependence is multi-group [47, 83, 92], which divides the frequency space into a small number of groups. We then evolve the specific intensities which are frequency integrated inside each group. Properly weighted opacities (such as the Rosseland mean and Planck mean) are normally needed for each frequency bin. This approach can cover the frequency space continuously to allow a better energy conservation when photons are redistributed in the frequency space. This is also the approach we will take. It can be used to handle physical processes that have a smooth dependence of frequency such as Compton scattering. However, it will not be able to handle line transport easily without a large number of frequency groups. One special type of multi-group RT uses the so called opacity distribution function method, which divides the frequency space based on the ordering of opacity as a function of frequency [67, 2, 87]. It can be used to handle strong opacity variations as a function of frequency efficiently. However, future development is still needed to account for the frequency change due to Doppler effects correctly.

Coherent Thomson scattering process is widely included in RT calculations, where photons and gas can only exchange momentum but not energy during each scattering process. However, in many astrophysical systems, incoherent Compton scattering, where photons and gas can exchange both energy and momentum, plays an important role to determine thermal properties of the plasma as well as spectrum properties of the radiation field. This includes thermal Compton with high temperature electrons (typically 10610^{6} K or above), or bulk Compton due to large turbulent or bulk velocities of electrons. For example, the corona regions in accretion disks around black holes, where Compton upscattering of disk photons by high temperature or non-thermal electrons are believed to be the dominant mechanism to produce the commonly observed hard X-rays [26, 76]. In Gamma-ray bursts [78, 93], supernova shock breakout [10, 75], X-ray pulsars [7] and polar cap accretion onto neutron stars [4, 89], Compton scatterings are all believed to play an important role to determine the spectrum properties. The well known Sunyave-Zel’dovich effect is also just due to inverse Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background by the high energy electrons in galaxy cluster [74, 60].

Various numerical techniques have been developed to calculate the Comptonized spectrum. One common approach is Monte Carlo based methods[56, 24, 14, 66, 62, 61], which are flexible and can handle the relativistic scattering kernel accurately. However, it is typically not efficient in the optically thick regime and it is also hard to include stimulated emission term, which is necessary to get the blackbody spectrum in thermal equilibrium. Deterministic methods by solving specific intensities along discrete rays based on either short or long characteristics have also been developed [30, 58, 49], which typically solve the Kompaneets equation for Compton scattering. Most of these codes solve the RT equation in the post processing way, which means properties of the plasma are froze while the radiation spectrum is calculated. In this paper, we want to develop a scheme that is able to couple the Compton process with the full time dependent evolution of radiation magneto-hydrodynamic equations together. The scheme needs to work accurately and efficiently for any optical depth regime. Stimulated emission needs to be included so that we can recover the blackbody spectrum in thermal equilibrium. A numerical scheme that is able to accurately follow the time dependent evolution of radiation and gas is also fundamentally different from post processing calculations, as we need to ensure total energy and momentum conservation accurately. We will show in the following sections that the algorithm developed here satisfies all these constrains.

In [32], we developed an implicit scheme that solves the time dependent, frequency integrated RT equation directly based on discrete ordinates. Here we extend the algorithm to include the frequency dependence via the multi-group approach. The extended algorithm has maintained all the properties of the original scheme but also allows frequency dependent opacities with very flexible decomposition of the frequency space in a conservative way. This paper is organized as follows. In section II, we describe how the frequency groups are transformed in different frames via Lorentz transformation, as well as the full multi-group radiation MHD equations to solve. Numerical implementations of the algorithm are described in section III. In section IV, series of tests are described to demonstrate the multi-group capability of the new algorithm. Performance of the algorithm and future extensions are discussed in section V.

II Equations

We will extend the frequency integrate RT equation based on discrete ordinates as described in [32] by including multiple frequency groups. This require changes to source terms and transformation of specific intensities as well as frequency space in different frames as shown in the following sections. One important property we always keep is that if only one frequency group is used, the formula will be automatically reduced to grey RT.

II.1 Frame Transformation For Multi-group Specific Intensities

The fundamental quantity we use to describes the radiation field is the lab frame specific intensity IνI_{\nu}, which is a function of time tt, spatial locations (x,y,z)(x,y,z), angular direction 𝒏n and monochromatic frequency ν\nu. We divide the frequency space into fixed NfN_{f} bins [0,ν1),[ν1,ν2),…​…,[νNf−2,νNf−1),[νNf−1,∞)[0,\nu_{1}),[\nu_{1},\nu_{2}),......,[\nu_{N_{f}-2},\nu_{N_{f}-1}),[\nu_{N_{f}-1},\infty) for Nf≥2N_{f}\geq 2. If Nf=1N_{f}=1, it will be just the whole frequency space [0,∞)[0,\infty). In each frequency bin [νf,νf+1)[\nu_{f},\nu_{f+1}), we define the frequency integrated specific intensity as

If≡∫νfνf+1Iν​𝑑ν.\displaystyle I_{f}\equiv\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}I_{\nu}d\nu. (1)

If we only have one frequency bin, this is reduced to the frequency integrated grey specific intensity. For the multi-group approach, we will evolve IfI_{f} as the discretized representation of IνI_{\nu} .

The numerical scheme will require transformation of specific intensities between lab frame and co-moving frame in order to solve the coupling terms between radiation and gas. Frequency ν\nu in the lab frame is related to the frequency in the co-moving frame ν0\nu_{0} as

II.2 The Angular Grid

The two types of angular grids mentioned in [32] are all currently supported for this multi-group RT algorithm and the implementation is identical. We summarize the notations here for completeness, which will also be used in the following sections. The first set of angles 𝒏n is defined with respect to fixed directions and they do not change with spatial location in the grid, even if the coordinate systems are curvilinear [8, 12]. The second set of angles is defined at fixed directions with respect to local coordinate axes in each cell. The direction vector 𝒏n itself will then change from cell to cell and additional terms are needed to account for this angular flux as described in section 3.2.4 of [32] following the formula given by [11]. This angular system can be very useful for simulations in spherical polar coordinate. In either angular grid, each angle 𝒏n has three components 𝒏=(nx,ny,nz){\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}=(n_{x},n_{y},n_{z}) and the corresponding quadrature weights wnw_{n} in the lab frame, which is determined by the angular volume 𝒏n represents. The commonly used radiation energy density ErE_{r}, flux 𝑭r{\mbox{\boldmath$F$}}_{r} and pressure 𝑷r{\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}_{r} are not needed in our RT equation. But they are useful diagnostics and can be constructed by angular quadrature of the specific intensities in each frequency bin as

Er,f\displaystyle E_{r,f} =\displaystyle= 4​π​∑n=0N−1If​(𝒏)​wn,\displaystyle 4\pi\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}I_{f}({\mbox{\boldmath$n$}})w_{n},
𝑭r,f\displaystyle{\mbox{\boldmath$F$}}_{r,f} =\displaystyle= 4​π​c​∑n=0N−1If​(𝒏)​𝒏​wn,\displaystyle 4\pi c\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}I_{f}({\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}){\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}w_{n},
𝑷r,f\displaystyle{\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}_{r,f} =\displaystyle= 4​π​∑n=0N−1If​(𝒏)​𝒏𝒏​wn,\displaystyle 4\pi\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}I_{f}({\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}){\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}w_{n}, (7)

where NN is the total number of angles per cell. Similar calculations can be done to get the moments in the co-moving frame except that we need to use the angles in the co-moving frame 𝒏′{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}^{\prime} and the co-moving frame quadrature weight wn′=Γ−2​wnw_{n}^{\prime}=\Gamma^{-2}w_{n} for co-moving frame specific intensities I0,f​(𝒏′)I_{0,f}({\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}^{\prime}). Frequency integrated moments of the radiation field are simply

Er=∑f=0Nf−1Er,f;𝑭r=∑f=0Nf−1𝑭r,f;𝑷r=∑f=0Nf−1𝑷r,f.\displaystyle E_{r}=\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}E_{r,f};{\mbox{\boldmath$F$}}_{r}=\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}{\mbox{\boldmath$F$}}_{r,f};{\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}_{r}=\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}{\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}_{r,f}. (8)

II.3 Equations for Multi-group RT

The lab frame monochromatic RT equation can be written as [47]

∂Iν∂t+c​𝒏⋅∇Iν=c⁡(ην−χν​Iν),\displaystyle\frac{\partial I_{\nu}}{\partial t}+c{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{\nu}=c\left(\eta_{\nu}-\chi_{\nu}I_{\nu}\right), (9)

where ην\eta_{\nu} and χν\chi_{\nu} are the monochromatic emissivity and opacity. We integrate the left and right hand sides over frequency for each bin [νf,νf+1)[\nu_{f},\nu_{f+1}) to get the equation we actually solve for frequency integrated specific intensities in each bin

∂If∂t+c​𝒏⋅∇If=c⁡(ηf−χf​If),\displaystyle\frac{\partial I_{f}}{\partial t}+c{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{f}=c\left(\eta_{f}-\chi_{f}I_{f}\right), (10)

where ηf≡∫νfνf+1ην​𝑑ν\eta_{f}\equiv\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}\eta_{\nu}d\nu and χf≡∫νfνf+1χν​Iν​𝑑ν/If\chi_{f}\equiv\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}\chi_{\nu}I_{\nu}d\nu/I_{f}. Expressions for the source terms in the co-moving frame can be determined in a similar way as done for grey RT [32]. We apply the frame transformation operator Γ4​(𝒏,𝒗)\Gamma^{4}({\mbox{\boldmath$n$}},{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}) to both sides of equation 10 and then the frequency mapping operator ℳν\mathcal{M}_{\nu}. We assume scattering, absorption and emission are isotropic in the fluid rest frame. All these terms are integrated over frequency for each group in the co-moving frame. The resulting source terms can be written as

∂I0,f∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial I_{0,f}}{\partial t} =\displaystyle= cΓ[ρκs(J0,f−I0,f)+ρκa,f(ε0,f−I0,f)\displaystyle c\Gamma\left[\right.\rho\kappa_{s}(J_{0,f}-I_{0,f})+\rho\kappa_{a,f}\left(\varepsilon_{0,f}-I_{0,f}\right) (11)
+\displaystyle+ ρ(κp,f−κa,f)(ε0,f−J0,f)]\displaystyle\rho(\kappa_{p,f}-\kappa_{a,f})\left(\varepsilon_{0,f}-J_{0,f}\right)\left.\right]
=\displaystyle= cΓ[ρ(κs+κa,f)(J0,f−I0,f)\displaystyle c\Gamma\left[\right.\rho\left(\kappa_{s}+\kappa_{a,f}\right)\left(J_{0,f}-I_{0,f}\right)
+\displaystyle+ ρκp,f(ε0,f−J0,f)].\displaystyle\rho\kappa_{p,f}\left(\varepsilon_{0,f}-J_{0,f}\right)\left.\right].

Here ε0,f\varepsilon_{0,f} is the frequency integrated thermal emissivity for each frequency bin. In principle, ε0,f\varepsilon_{0,f} can be any function of local gas and radiation properties. Our default assumption is local thermal equilibrium so that ε0,f\varepsilon_{0,f} is determined by the gas temperature TT as

ε0,f\displaystyle\varepsilon_{0,f} =\displaystyle= 14​π​∫νfνf+1B⁡(ν,T)​𝑑ν,\displaystyle\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}B(\nu,T)d\nu,
=\displaystyle= 14​π​∫h​νf/kB​Th​νf+1/kB​TB⁡(νT)​d​νT,\displaystyle\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{h\nu_{f}/k_{B}T}^{h\nu_{f+1}/k_{B}T}B(\nu_{T})d\nu_{T},
B⁡(ν,T)\displaystyle B(\nu,T) =\displaystyle= 8​π​h​ν3c3​1exp⁡(h​ν/kB​T)−1,\displaystyle\frac{8\pi h\nu^{3}}{c^{3}}\frac{1}{\exp\left(h\nu/k_{B}T\right)-1},
B⁡(νT)\displaystyle B(\nu_{T}) =\displaystyle= 15​ar​T4π4​νT3exp⁡(νT)−1.\displaystyle\frac{15a_{r}T^{4}}{\pi^{4}}\frac{\nu_{T}^{3}}{\exp(\nu_{T})-1}. (12)

We have defined the dimensionless frequency as νT≡h​ν/kB​T\nu_{T}\equiv h\nu/k_{B}T and ara_{r} is the radiation constant while kBk_{B} is the Boltzmann constant. It can be easily checked that if we only have one frequency bin, ε0,f\varepsilon_{0,f} is reduced to the normal thermal emission term ε0,f=ar​T4/(4​π)\varepsilon_{0,f}=a_{r}T^{4}/\left(4\pi\right). The mean radiation energy density in each frequency bin J0J_{0} is just the angular quadrature of the specific intensities as

J0,f=∫I0,f​d​Ω0,\displaystyle J_{0,f}=\int I_{0,f}d\Omega_{0}, (13)

where Ω0\Omega_{0} is the weight of angular quadrature in the co-moving frame. This can be done because co-moving frame specific intensities I0,fI_{0,f} share the same frequency grid νf\nu_{f} for different angles. Scattering opacity κs\kappa_{s} is typically taken to be the electron scattering value while the Rosseland mean (κa,f\kappa_{a,f}) and Planck mean (κp,f\kappa_{p,f}) absorption opacities in each frequency bin are defined as

1κa,f\displaystyle\frac{1}{\kappa_{a,f}} ≡\displaystyle\equiv 1∫νfνf+1BT​(ν,T)​𝑑ν​∫νfνf+11κa,ν​BT​(ν,T)​𝑑ν,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}B_{T}(\nu,T)d\nu}\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}\frac{1}{\kappa_{a,\nu}}B_{T}(\nu,T)d\nu,
κp,f\displaystyle\kappa_{p,f} ≡\displaystyle\equiv 1∫νfνf+1B⁡(ν,T)​𝑑ν​∫νfνf+1κa,ν​B​(ν,T)​𝑑ν,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}B(\nu,T)d\nu}\int_{\nu_{f}}^{\nu_{f+1}}\kappa_{a,\nu}B(\nu,T)d\nu,
BT​(ν,T)\displaystyle B_{T}(\nu,T) ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∂B⁡(ν,T)∂T.\displaystyle\frac{\partial B(\nu,T)}{\partial T}. (14)

Here κa,ν\kappa_{a,\nu} is the absorption opacity at the monochromatic frequency ν\nu. If the integral is taken between [0,∞)[0,\infty), they are the commonly used Rosseland mean and Planck mean opacities in grey RT. The opacities are defined in the co-moving frame but the integral is done for the frequency grid νf\nu_{f}.

These source terms only include isotropic scattering and radiation energy density does not change during the scattering process. Additional terms need to be added to account for Compton scattering, which is described in the following section II.4. We have also approximated the specific intensity weighted opacities with the Rosseland mean and Planck mean values [54], as χf\chi_{f} is generally unavailable. It can be easily confirmed that if we integrate the specific intensities over all angles in the co-moving frame, κs+κa,f\kappa_{s}+\kappa_{a,f} will determine the momentum coupling between photons and gas while only κp,f\kappa_{p,f} will be responsible for the thermal coupling as expected. Notice that if we can use large enough number of frequency bins to resolve the frequency dependence of opacities, κa,f\kappa_{a,f} and κp,f\kappa_{p,f} will both approach κa,ν\kappa_{a,\nu} and the term (κp,f−κa,f)​(ε0,f−J0,f)(\kappa_{p,f}-\kappa_{a,f})\left(\varepsilon_{0,f}-J_{0,f}\right) will go away.

II.4 Kompaneets Equation for Compton Scattering

In the limit that h​ν,kB​T≪me​c2h\nu,\ k_{B}T\ll m_{e}c^{2}, Kompaneets equation [38] can be used to describe the energy exchange between photons and gas via Compton scattering. Although full angular dependent Compton scattering kernel can be used as in many Monte Carlo calculations [56, 59, 30], it significantly complicates the equation and makes the scheme much more expensive. Instead, we will assume that the energy exchange due to Compton scattering is uniformly distributed over all angles in the co-moving frame of the gas, which should be a good assumption when radiation flux is much smaller than c​ErcE_{r}. Therefore the momentum exchange between photon and gas is described by the usual scattering term, which is already included in equation 11.

The Kompaneets equation evolves the photon occupation number nνn_{\nu}, which is related to the monochromatic radiation energy density JνJ_{\nu} as

nν=(c38​π​h)​Jνν3,\displaystyle n_{\nu}=\left(\frac{c^{3}}{8\pi h}\right)\frac{J_{\nu}}{\nu^{3}}, (15)

Evolution of nνn_{\nu} due to Compton scattering follows this equation

1c​ρ​κes​∂nν∂t=kB​Tme​c2​1νT2​∂∂νT​(νT4​[∂nν∂νT+nν​(nν+1)]),\frac{1}{c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}}\frac{\partial n_{\nu}}{\partial t}=\frac{k_{B}T}{m_{e}c^{2}}\frac{1}{\nu_{T}^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu_{T}}\left(\nu_{T}^{4}\left[\frac{\partial n_{\nu}}{\partial\nu_{T}}+n_{\nu}(n_{\nu}+1)\right]\right), (16)

where κes\kappa_{\rm es} is the frequency independent electron scattering value. We assume gas temperature is fixed while this equation is solved. Then we can change the independent variable from νT\nu_{T} to the dimensionless frequency ν~≡h​ν/kB​T0\tilde{\nu}\equiv h\nu/k_{B}T_{0}, which is independent of gas temperature TT, as

1c​ρ​κes​∂nν~∂t=1Te​1ν~2​∂∂ν~​(ν~4​[T​∂nν~∂ν~+nν~​(nν~+1)]),\frac{1}{c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}}\frac{\partial n_{\tilde{\nu}}}{\partial t}=\frac{1}{T_{e}}\frac{1}{\tilde{\nu}^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{\nu}}\left(\tilde{\nu}^{4}\left[T\frac{\partial n_{\tilde{\nu}}}{\partial\tilde{\nu}}+n_{\tilde{\nu}}(n_{\tilde{\nu}}+1)\right]\right), (17)

where we have defined Te≡me​c2/kB​T0T_{e}\equiv m_{e}c^{2}/k_{B}T_{0} and gas temperature TT is scaled with our fiducial temperature unit T0T_{0}.

Numerically, we will implement a conservative format of the above equation for total photon numbers N=∫nν~​ν~2​𝑑ν~N=\int n_{\tilde{\nu}}\tilde{\nu}^{2}d\tilde{\nu} as

Tec​ρ​κes​∂(ν~2​nν~)∂t=∂∂ν~​[ν~4​F​(nν~)],\displaystyle\frac{T_{e}}{c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}}\frac{\partial\left(\tilde{\nu}^{2}n_{\tilde{\nu}}\right)}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\tilde{\nu}}\left[\tilde{\nu}^{4}F(n_{\tilde{\nu}})\right], (18)

which describes the process that photons are just transported between different frequency bins with the flux ν~4​F​(nν~)\tilde{\nu}^{4}F(n_{\tilde{\nu}}) and

F⁡(nν~)≡T​∂nν~∂ν~+nν~​(nν~+1).\displaystyle F(n_{\tilde{\nu}})\equiv T\frac{\partial n_{\tilde{\nu}}}{\partial\tilde{\nu}}+n_{\tilde{\nu}}\left(n_{\tilde{\nu}}+1\right). (19)

The first term represents diffusion in the frequency space while the non-linear term nν~2n_{\tilde{\nu}}^{2} is due to stimulated emission. In steady state, F⁡(nν~)F(n_{\tilde{\nu}}) needs to be zero for all frequency bins and the general Bose-Einstein distribution nν~=1/[λ​exp⁡(ν~/T)−1]n_{\tilde{\nu}}=1/\left[\lambda\exp(\tilde{\nu}/T)-1\right] satisfies this condition. Blackbody distribution is just a special case with λ=1\lambda=1. Notice that if the stimulated emission term nν~2n_{\tilde{\nu}}^{2} is not included, the steady state spectrum will take the Wien distribution nν~∝exp(−ν~/T)n_{\tilde{\nu}}\propto\exp{\left(-\tilde{\nu}/T\right)}.

The change of mean radiation energy density due to Compton process can be determined by integrating the left and right hand sides of equation 17 with ν~4​d​ν~\tilde{\nu}^{4}d\tilde{\nu}. It can be shown that if the gas temperature TT equals the Compton temperature TcT_{c} (in unit of T0T_{0}) of the radiation field as defined in the following way

Tc≡(∫0∞nν~ν~3dν~)−1[14∫0∞nν~ν~4dν~\displaystyle T_{c}\equiv\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}n_{\tilde{\nu}}\tilde{\nu}^{3}d\tilde{\nu}\right)^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\infty}n_{\tilde{\nu}}\tilde{\nu}^{4}d\tilde{\nu}\right.
+π460∫0∞nν~2ν~4dν~],\displaystyle+\left.\frac{\pi^{4}}{60}\int_{0}^{\infty}n_{\tilde{\nu}}^{2}\tilde{\nu}^{4}d\tilde{\nu}\right], (20)

there will be no change of the mean radiation energy density for any spectrum.

In section III.3, we will describe how this Kompaneets equation is used to determine the change of I0,fI_{0,f} numerically. In principle, equation 17 can be converted to an equation that evolves JνJ_{\nu} directly as done in [30]. However, we prefer the current format to evolve photon number density as it has a nice conservation property for the Compton process.

II.5 Full Equations for Multi-group Radiation MHD

Radiation energy and momentum source terms for the gas are simply the sum of contributions from photons in all frequency bins. In the lab frame, the total energy and momentum of gas and radiation are conserved. For completeness, we summarize the full multi-group radiation MHD equations as

∂ρ∂t+∇⋅(ρ​𝒗)\displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}\cdot(\rho{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}) =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
∂(ρ​𝒗)∂t+∇⋅(ρ​𝒗𝒗−𝑩𝑩+𝖯∗)\displaystyle\frac{\partial(\rho{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}})}{\partial t}+{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}\cdot({\rho{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}-{\mbox{\boldmath$B$}}{\mbox{\boldmath$B$}}+{{\sf P}^{\ast}}}) =\displaystyle= −∑f=0Nf−1𝑺f(𝑷),\displaystyle-\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}\bm{S}_{f}({\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}),\
∂E∂t+∇⋅[(E+P∗)​𝒗−𝑩⁡(𝑩⋅𝒗)]\displaystyle\frac{\partial{E}}{\partial t}+{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}\cdot\left[(E+P^{\ast}){\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}-{\mbox{\boldmath$B$}}({\mbox{\boldmath$B$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}})\right] =\displaystyle= −∑f=0Nf−1Sf(E),\displaystyle-\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}S_{f}(E),
∂𝑩∂t−∇×(𝒗×𝑩)\displaystyle\frac{\partial{\mbox{\boldmath$B$}}}{\partial t}-{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}\times({\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}\times{\mbox{\boldmath$B$}}) =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (21)

Here ρ,𝒗,P\rho,{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}},P and 𝑩B are density, flow velocity, gas pressure and the magnetic field respectively with the total pressure 𝖯∗≡(P+B2/2)​𝖨{\sf P}^{\ast}\equiv(P+B^{2}/2){\sf I} ( 𝖨{\sf I} is the unit tensor). Ideal MHD has been assumed for the induction equation. Total energy density is defined as

E=Eg+12​ρ​v2+B22,\displaystyle E=E_{g}+\frac{1}{2}\rho v^{2}+\frac{B^{2}}{2}, (22)

where gas internal energy is Eg=P/(γg−1)E_{g}=P/(\gamma_{g}-1) for the adiabatic index γg≠1\gamma_{g}\neq 1. The gas temperature is calculated with T=(μ​mp/kB)​(P/ρ)T=\left(\mu m_{p}/k_{B}\right)\left(P/\rho\right), where μ\mu is the mean molecular weight and mpm_{p} is the proton mass. Momentum and energy source terms due to photons in each frequency group are represented by 𝑺f​(𝑷)\bm{S}_{f}({\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}) and Sf​(E)S_{f}(E).

The corresponding equations for specific intensities are

∂If∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial I_{f}}{\partial t} +\displaystyle+ c​𝒏⋅∇If=c​Sf​(I),\displaystyle c{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{f}=cS_{f}(I),
Sf​(I)\displaystyle S_{f}(I) ≡\displaystyle\equiv Γ−3ℳν−1[ρ(κs+κa,f)(J0,f−I0,f)\displaystyle\Gamma^{-3}\mathcal{M}_{\nu}^{-1}\left[\right.\rho(\kappa_{s}+\kappa_{a,f})\left(J_{0,f}-I_{0,f}\right)
+\displaystyle+ ρκp,f(ε0,f−J0,f)+Sc(If)],\displaystyle\rho\kappa_{p,f}\left(\varepsilon_{0,f}-J_{0,f}\right)+S_{c}(I_{f})\left.\right],
I0,f\displaystyle I_{0,f} =\displaystyle= ℳν​Γ4​If,\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\nu}\Gamma^{4}I_{f},
Sf​(E)\displaystyle S_{f}(E) ≡\displaystyle\equiv 4​π​c​∫Sf​(I)​𝑑Ω,\displaystyle 4\pi c\int S_{f}(I)d\Omega,
𝑺f​(𝑷)\displaystyle\bm{S}_{f}({\mbox{\boldmath$P$}}) ≡\displaystyle\equiv 4​π​∫𝒏​Sf​(I)​𝑑Ω,\displaystyle 4\pi\int{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}S_{f}(I)d\Omega, (23)

where Sc​(If)S_{c}(I_{f}) is the source term due to Compton scattering, which will be described in Section III.3. The weight of angular quadrature in the lab frame d​Ωd\Omega is also normalized such that ∫𝑑Ω=1\int d\Omega=1.

This set of RT equations is basically the Newtonian version of the covariant RT equation derived by [11] after we integrate specific intensities over frequency inside each frequency bin. Notice that we can use any frequency grid and Doppler shift in the frequency space is not just limited to neighboring bins but can happen in multiple bins between the two different sets of frequency grids νf\nu_{f} and ν0,f\nu_{0,f} in the co-moving frame. Multi-frequency radiation moment equations can be also derived by integrating specific intensities over the angles [46, 83, 91, 1]. These equations will need closure relations for the second and third moments of specific intensities in order to evolve the frequency dependent radiation energy density and flux. In contrast, our equations evolving specific intensities are closed and no additional closure assumption is needed.

III Numerical Algorithm

Our numerical scheme to solve this set of multi-group radiation MHD equations is a natural extension of the implicit solver for grey RT as described in [32]. The transport term c​𝒏⋅∇Ifc{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{f} for different frequency groups is independent of each other, which is one big advantage of evolving specific intensities in the lab frame. This term is discretized in the same way as described in Section 3.2.1 of [32] and we will not repeat here. Before we describe how the source terms in different frequency groups are coupled together as well as the Compton terms, we will first give an overview of the basic steps.

III.1 Steps of the Multi-Group Radiation MHD Scheme

The numerical scheme described below is for the second order Van-Leer integrator with predict-correct steps in Athena++ [72]. Details for some of the steps will be described in the following sections.

  1. Step 1:

    Set up the spatial mesh grid for both the fluid and radiation field. Choose angular and frequency grids for specific intensities. Initialize both MHD and radiation variables. Calculate time step Δ​t\Delta t based on the standard Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition for MHD.

  2. Step 2:

    Evolve the MHD equations for half time step Δ​t/2\Delta t/2 using the standard MHD integrator in Athena++.

  3. Step 3:

    Construct the matrix coefficients for the RT equation with half time step Δ​t/2\Delta t/2 based on fluid variables at the beginning of the step. The coefficients will include contributions from the transport term as well as the source term Sf​(I)S_{f}(I).

  4. Step 4:

    Solve the RT equation iteratively for specific intensities until a desired precision is achieved. The change of specific intensities due to the Compton term Sc​(I)S_{c}(I) is also added in the co-moving frame during the iteration.

  5. Step 5:

    Add radiation energy and momentum source terms to the gas based on total energy and momentum conservation to get the final gas properties in the predict step.

  6. Step 6:

    Repeat steps 2 to 5 to update both MHD and radiation variables for a full time step Δ​t\Delta t.

III.2 Implicit Solver for Multi-group RT

For any step mm, we start with the initial condition of gas and radiation field given by ρm,Tm,𝒗m\rho^{m},T^{m},{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}^{m} and IfmI_{f}^{m}. Then we have the following equations to advance the radiation field to the next step m+1m+1 by time step Δ​t\Delta t with the change of gas internal energy as

Ifm+1−Ifm+Δ​t​c​𝒏⋅∇Ifm+1=\displaystyle I_{f}^{m+1}-I_{f}^{m}+\Delta tc{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{f}^{m+1}=

This is a set of equations for Nf×N×Nx×Ny×NzN_{f}\times N\times N_{x}\times N_{y}\times N_{z} specific intensities plus gas temperature, where Nx,Ny,NzN_{x},N_{y},N_{z} are total number of cells along three spatial coordinates. Notice that we have assumed the opacity and emissivity are independent of angles in the co-moving frame but they can depend on frequencies. This can be reorganized to an equation for J0,f,lm+1J_{0,f,l}^{m+1} as

(1−A1,f)​J0,f,lm+1=A2,f​ε0,f,lm+1+A3,f,\displaystyle(1-A_{1,f})J_{0,f,l}^{m+1}=A_{2,f}\varepsilon_{0,f,l}^{m+1}+A_{3,f}, (31)

where the coefficients are defined as

This can be used to get the equation for gas temperature as

ρm​kB(γg−1)​μ​mp​(Tlm+1−Tm)=−γ​4​π​Δ​t​c​ρm\displaystyle\frac{\rho^{m}k_{B}}{\left(\gamma_{g}-1\right)\mu m_{p}}\left(T^{m+1}_{l}-T^{m}\right)=-\gamma 4\pi\Delta tc\rho^{m}
×∑f=0Nf−1κp,f​[1−A1,f−A2,f1−A1,f​ε0,f,lm+1−A3,f1−A1,f].\displaystyle\times\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}\kappa_{p,f}\left[\frac{1-A_{1,f}-A_{2,f}}{1-A_{1,f}}\varepsilon_{0,f,l}^{m+1}-\frac{A_{3,f}}{1-A_{1,f}}\right]. (33)

For our default emissivity given by equation 25, ε0,f,lm+1\varepsilon_{0,f,l}^{m+1} is a function of Tlm+1T^{m+1}_{l}, which can be determined by the above equation. For the case of one frequency bin (grey approximation), it is a fourth order polynomial for Tlm+1T_{l}^{m+1} and we can find the root easily. For the general case, we need to solve the equation iteratively as ε¯0,f,l≡ε0,f,lm+1/(Tlm+1)4\overline{\varepsilon}_{0,f,l}\equiv\varepsilon_{0,f,l}^{m+1}/\left(T_{l}^{m+1}\right)^{4} is also a function of Tlm+1T_{l}^{m+1}. We first calculate ε¯0,f,l\overline{\varepsilon}_{0,f,l} for each frequency bin using Tl−1m+1T_{l-1}^{m+1} and solve equation 33 to get an estimate for Tlm+1T_{l}^{m+1}. Then we use this estimated temperature to update ε¯0,f,l\overline{\varepsilon}_{0,f,l} and improve the solution for Tlm+1T_{l}^{m+1}. It typically takes a few iterations to get a solution to equation 33 with relative error smaller than 10−610^{-6}. With this solution, we calculate J0,f,lm+1J_{0,f,l}^{m+1} according to equation 31 and then get I0,f,lm+1I_{0,f,l}^{m+1} according to equation 29. After that, we update I0,f,lm+1I_{0,f,l}^{m+1} with the Compton source term ScS_{c} if necessary and the updated solution is labeled as I0,f,lm′+1I_{0,f,l}^{m^{\prime}+1}. The detailed process to solve the Kompaneets equation is described in Section III.3. Finally, we get the lab frame specific intensity as If,lm+1=Γ−4​ℳν−1​I0,f,lm′+1I_{f,l}^{m+1}=\Gamma^{-4}\mathcal{M}_{\nu}^{-1}I_{0,f,l}^{m^{\prime}+1}. This finishes one iterative step and we continue this iteration for the whole simulation domain until the relative error Δ​I\Delta I is smaller than a preset criterion, where Δ​I\Delta I is defined as

Δ​I≡∑f,n,i,j,k|If,lm+1−If,l−1m+1|/∑f,n,i,j,kIf,lm+1.\displaystyle\Delta I\equiv\sum_{f,n,i,j,k}|I^{m+1}_{f,l}-I^{m+1}_{f,l-1}|/\sum_{f,n,i,j,k}I^{m+1}_{f,l}. (34)

Here the sum is done over the whole simulation domain and for all angles and frequency bins. We also support the stopping criterion that the maximum relative error |If,lm+1−If,l−1m+1|/If,lm+1|I^{m+1}_{f,l}-I^{m+1}_{f,l-1}|/I^{m+1}_{f,l} is smaller than a preset value.

After we update all the lab frame specific intensities to time step m+1m+1, we determine the radiation energy and momentum source terms that we need to deposit to the gas based on total energy and momentum conservation in the lab frame in the same way as described in section 3.2.3 of [32]. The source terms include contributions from all frequency bins. This will automatically capture all the velocity dependent source terms caused by Lorentz transformation.

III.3 Kompaneets Solver for Compton Scattering

In this section, we will describe how the Kompaneets equation 17 is solved to account for the change of specific intensities in the co-moving frame due to Compton scattering during each iterative step. The Kompaneets equation is solved with a conservative implicit approach following [9]. We use gas temperature Tlm+1T^{m+1}_{l} from each iterative step and assume it is a constant while the Kompaneets equation is solved. The initial condition of this solver is I0,f,lm+1I^{m+1}_{0,f,l} and the associated J0,f,lm+1J^{m+1}_{0,f,l} as described in last section before the Compton source term ScS_{c} is added. Without loss of generality for each iterative step ll and time step mm, we will drop subscript ll and upper script m+1m+1 for these quantities. For simplicity, we will also use dimensionless frequency ν~≡h​ν/(kB​T0)\tilde{\nu}\equiv h\nu/\left(k_{B}T_{0}\right) for a fiducial temperature unit T0T_{0}.

For frequency bins 00 to Nf−2N_{f}-2, we estimate the photon occupation number nf+1/2n_{f+1/2} at the center of each frequency bin [ν~f,ν~f+1)[\tilde{\nu}_{f},\tilde{\nu}_{f+1}) according to equation 15 with the monochromatic radiation energy density estimated as J0,f/(ν~f+1−ν~f)J_{0,f}/(\tilde{\nu}_{f+1}-\tilde{\nu}_{f}). For the last frequency bin ν~∈[ν~Nf−1,∞)\tilde{\nu}\in[\tilde{\nu}_{N_{f}-1},\infty), we assume the photon occupation number follows the spectrum shape nν~∝exp(−ν~/T)n_{\tilde{\nu}}\propto\exp(-\tilde{\nu}/T) with the normalization fixed by the requirement that ∫νNf−1∞J0,ν​𝑑ν\int_{\nu_{N_{f}-1}}^{\infty}J_{0,\nu}d\nu should match J0,Nf−1J_{0,N_{f}-1} .

In order to calculate the fluxes F⁡(nν~)F(n_{\tilde{\nu}}), we need to get the values of nfn_{f} at the faces of each frequency bin, which are determined based on reconstruction of nf−1/2n_{f-1/2} and nf+1/2n_{f+1/2} as

nf=δf​nf−1/2+(1−δf)​nf+1/2.\displaystyle n_{f}=\delta_{f}n_{f-1/2}+(1-\delta_{f})n_{f+1/2}. (35)

The following steps adopt the procedure described by [9] to determine the coefficient δf\delta_{f}. We first calculate the total photon numbers N=∑f=0Nf−1nf+1/2​ν~f+1/22​(ν~f+1−ν~f)N=\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}n_{f+1/2}\tilde{\nu}_{f+1/2}^{2}(\tilde{\nu}_{f+1}-\tilde{\nu}_{f}). Notice that for the last frequency bin, we just take the integral with the assumed spectrum shape. The steady state solution is n~ν~=1/(λ​exp⁡[ν~/T]−1)\tilde{n}_{\tilde{\nu}}=1/(\lambda\exp[\tilde{\nu}/T]-1) and the coefficient λ\lambda is determined by the following constrain

∫0∞ν~2λ​exp⁡[ν~/T]−1​𝑑ν~=N.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\tilde{\nu}^{2}}{\lambda\exp[\tilde{\nu}/T]-1}d\tilde{\nu}=N. (36)

We require that the condition F⁡(n~ν~)=0F(\tilde{n}_{\tilde{\nu}})=0 (equation 19) is satisfied in the current frequency grid, which means

T​n~f+1/2−n~f−1/2ν~f+1/2−ν~f−1/2+n~f​(n~f+1)=0.\displaystyle T\frac{\tilde{n}_{f+1/2}-\tilde{n}_{f-1/2}}{\tilde{\nu}_{f+1/2}-\tilde{\nu}_{f-1/2}}+\tilde{n}_{f}\left(\tilde{n}_{f}+1\right)=0. (37)

This will result in a second order polynomial equation for δf\delta_{f}, which only has one root between 00 and 0.50.5. Notice that the steady state solution is only used to determine the reconstruction coefficients δf\delta_{f}. Time dependent evolution of the spectrum is fully captured.

We solve the Kompaneets equation implicitly to make sure the scheme is stable in the optically thick regime when the Compton thermalization timescale is shorter than the time step. We start with the photon occupation number nf+1/2m′n_{f+1/2}^{m^{\prime}} as determined by the partially updated co-moving frame J0,f,lm+1J_{0,f,l}^{m+1} as described in the last section. Then we update them with the following equation

Tec​ρ​κes​ν~f+1/22​(ν~f+1−ν~f−1)​nf+1/2m′+1−nf+1/2m′γ​Δ​t=\displaystyle\frac{T_{e}}{c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}}\tilde{\nu}_{f+1/2}^{2}\left(\tilde{\nu}_{f+1}-\tilde{\nu}_{f-1}\right)\frac{n_{f+1/2}^{m^{\prime}+1}-n_{f+1/2}^{m^{\prime}}}{\gamma\Delta t}=
ν~f+14​F​(nf+1m′+1)−ν~f4​F​(nfm′+1).\displaystyle\tilde{\nu}^{4}_{f+1}F\left(n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{f+1}\right)-\tilde{\nu}^{4}_{f}F\left(n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{f}\right). (38)

The flux is calculated at the boundary of frequency bins using updated photon occupation number nf+1/2m′+1n_{f+1/2}^{m^{\prime}+1} except the stimulated emission term, which is calculated using nf+1/2m′n_{f+1/2}^{m^{\prime}}. This means

F⁡(nfm′+1)\displaystyle F\left(n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{f}\right) =\displaystyle= T​nf+1/2m′+1−nf−1/2m′+1ν~f+1/2−ν~f−1/2\displaystyle T\frac{n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{{f+1/2}}-n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{f-1/2}}{\tilde{\nu}_{f+1/2}-\tilde{\nu}_{f-1/2}} (39)
+\displaystyle+ nfm′+1​(1+nfm).\displaystyle n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{f}\left(1+n^{m}_{f}\right).

For the last frequency bin, we calculate the gradient using nNf−3/2m′+1n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{N_{f}-3/2} and nNf−1m′n^{m^{\prime}}_{N_{f}-1}. However, if nNf−3/2m′<nNf−1m′n_{N_{f}-3/2}^{m^{\prime}}<n^{m^{\prime}}_{N_{f}-1}, we simply set the flux at ν~Nf−1\tilde{\nu}_{N_{f}-1} to be 0. The flux at the frequency boundary ν~0=0\tilde{\nu}_{0}=0 is also set to be 0. This results in a set of linear equations with respect to nf+1/2m′+1n^{m^{\prime}+1}_{f+1/2}, which can be easily solved with Gauss elimination.

Once we have the updated solution for nf+1/2m′+1n_{f+1/2}^{m^{\prime}+1}, we can get the updated mean radiation energy density J0,f,lm′+1J_{0,f,l}^{m^{\prime}+1}. Finally, the co-moving frame specific intensities are updated as

I0,f,lm′+1=I0,f,lm+1+(J0,f,lm′+1−J0,f,lm+1).\displaystyle I_{0,f,l}^{m^{\prime}+1}=I_{0,f,l}^{m+1}+(J_{0,f,l}^{m^{\prime}+1}-J_{0,f,l}^{m+1}). (40)

IV Numerical Tests

The algorithm for multi-group radiation MHD developed here is designed to recover the grey approximation when one frequency bin is used, or if the conditions (initial condition, boundary condition and opacities) in all frequency bins are identical. We will not repeat all the tests that are already carried out in [32]. Instead, we will focus on testing the new multi-group features, including frequency dependent opacities and emissivities, Doppler effects as well as the Kompaneets solver for Compton scattering. Since we will only be able to afford a small number of frequency groups for real applications, all the tests will use broad frequency groups instead of sharp features in the frequency space such as lines. RT with opacities due to atomic lines can be also modeled in the framework developed here in principle. However, too many frequency groups will be needed to resolve the Doppler shift of lines to make it feasible in practice. We will discuss future extensions to model line transport more efficiently in section V.

Results of the following tests will be reported in dimensionless numbers with assumed temperature, density, and length units to be T0T_{0}, ρ0\rho_{0}, and L0L_{0}, respectively. The velocity unit v0v_{0} is the isothermal sound speed at temperature T0T_{0} and time unit will be L0/v0L_{0}/v_{0}. When we refer to a logarithmic frequency grid with NfN_{f} frequency groups for [ν~l,ν~r][\tilde{\nu}_{l},\tilde{\nu}_{r}] in the following tests, we always mean two groups cover [0,ν~l)[0,\tilde{\nu}_{l}) and [ν~r,∞)[\tilde{\nu}_{r},\infty) respectively and the rest Nf−2N_{f}-2 groups cover the range [ν~l,ν~r)[\tilde{\nu}_{l},\tilde{\nu}_{r}) with logarithmic frequency spacing. Two dimensionless numbers that can convert the dimensionless numbers to physical units are ℂ=c/v0{\mathbb{C}}=c/v_{0} and ℙ=ar​T04​μ​mp/(ρ0​kB​T0){\mathbb{P}}=a_{r}T_{0}^{4}\mu m_{p}/(\rho_{0}k_{B}T_{0}) [34], which we will report for each test problem. Gas adiabatic index is taken to be γg=5/3\gamma_{g}=5/3 unless otherwise specified. If not specified, we will assume local gas emission follows the blackbody spectrum (equation 12).

IV.1 Thermal Equilibrium of Multi-group Source Terms

To test our solver for the source terms particularly when opacity varies significantly with frequencies, we create a 2D uniform box covering the region [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]\times[0,1] with spatial resolution 32×3232\times 32. We use three frequency bins ν~∈[0,4),[4,8),[8,∞)\tilde{\nu}\in[0,4),[4,8),[8,\infty) and the Planck mean absorption opacity in each bin is taken to be ρ0​κp​L0=100,200,300\rho_{0}\kappa_{p}L_{0}=100,200,300 respectively. The units are chosen so that ℙ=1{\mathbb{P}}=1 and ℂ=10{\mathbb{C}}=10. Density and temperature of the gas are set to be 11 initially while the initial mean radiation energy density in the three frequency bins are Er,0/ar​T04=10,Er,1/ar​T04=20E_{r,0}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4}=10,E_{r,1}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4}=20 and Er,3/ar​T04=30E_{r,3}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4}=30. The thermalization timescales in all three frequency bins are smaller than the time step and solution reach steady state quickly as shown in Figure 2. Analytical solution in steady state can be calculated based on total energy conservation and the requirement that 4​π​ε0,f4\pi\varepsilon_{0,f} needs to match Er,fE_{r,f} in each frequency bin. The gas temperature in steady state is T=2.75T=2.75 and the emissivity in the three frequency bins are 4​π​ε0,0/ar​T04=5.07,4​π​ε0,1/ar​T04=16.30,4​π​ε0,2/ar​T04=36.004\pi\varepsilon_{0,0}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4}=5.07,4\pi\varepsilon_{0,1}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4}=16.30,4\pi\varepsilon_{0,2}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4}=36.00, which agree with the radiation energy density in each bin as well as the analytical solution. Since frequency bins are fixed, the ratio ε0,f/ar​T4\varepsilon_{0,f}/a_{r}T^{4} also changes with TT. In this test problem, it only takes five iterations of the polynomial solver to get the updated gas temperature to the non-linear equation 33.

IV.2 Radiating Sphere

One useful test of the multi-group RT scheme is to compare the numerical and analytical solutions to the radiating sphere problem as proposed by [25]. This test is done in one dimensional spherical polar coordinate covering the radial range r∈[0.02,0.05]r\in[0.02,0.05] with 3232 uniformly spaced grid points. Gas temperature is fixed to be Tg=0.03T_{g}=0.03 with the temperature unit chosen so that the dimensionless speed of light ℂ=805.9{\mathbb{C}}=805.9. Gas velocity is 0 and it does not evolve in this test. At the inner boundary ri=0.02r_{i}=0.02, specific intensities are set to be isotropic with a blackbody spectrum at temperature Tl=0.3T_{l}=0.3. At the outer boundary r=0.05r=0.05, we simply copy all outgoing specific intensities from the last active zone to the ghost zones while set all incoming specific intensities to be 0. The absorption opacity coefficient ρ​κa,f\rho\kappa_{a,f} is uniform in the whole simulation domain. Its dependence on frequency is tabulated by [25], which is also shown in the top panel of Figure 3. We use the second angular system as mentioned in section II.2 with 40 angles covering 180∘180^{\circ} with respect to the radial direction. Logarithmic frequency spacing is used to cover [3×10−3,29.9][3\times 10^{-3},29.9] with Nf=52N_{f}=52. Isotropic specific intensities are initialized in the simulation domain with blackbody spectrum at temperature TgT_{g}. Then radiation energy density at each radius rr and at any time tt is given by the following analytical solution [25]

Er​(ν~)\displaystyle E_{r}(\tilde{\nu}) =\displaystyle= [B⁡(ν~,Tl)−B⁡(ν~,Tg)]​fν~​(r,t)+B⁡(ν~,Tg),\displaystyle\left[B(\tilde{\nu},T_{l})-B(\tilde{\nu},T_{g})\right]f_{\tilde{\nu}}(r,t)+B(\tilde{\nu},T_{g}), (41)

where the function fν~​(r,t)f_{\tilde{\nu}}(r,t) is defined based on the relative values of ℂ​t{\mathbb{C}}t and r−rir-r_{i}. The solution is basically the sum of local blackbody emission at temperature TgT_{g} and the attenuated blackbody radiation from the inner boundary rir_{i} with temperature TlT_{l} if the distance between the inner boundary and current location is smaller than ℂ​t{\mathbb{C}}t. Therefore, when ℂ​t<r−R{\mathbb{C}}t<r-R, Fν~​(r,t)=0F_{\tilde{\nu}}(r,t)=0. For r−ri<ℂ​t<r2−ri2r-r_{i}<{\mathbb{C}}t<\sqrt{r^{2}-r_{i}^{2}}, we have

+\displaystyle+ [1ri​σν~−riℂ​t​(r2ri2−1)]​exp⁡(−σν~​ℂ​t)\displaystyle\left[\frac{1}{r_{i}\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}}}-\frac{r_{i}}{{\mathbb{C}}t}\left(\frac{r^{2}}{r_{i}^{2}}-1\right)\right]\exp\left(-\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}}{\mathbb{C}}t\right)

−\displaystyle- H(σν~ℂt)]},\displaystyle\left.\left.H(\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}}{\mathbb{C}}t)\right]\right\},

where we have defined the opacity coefficient σν~≡ρ​κa​(ν~)\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}}\equiv\rho\kappa_{a}(\tilde{\nu}) and the exponential integral

H⁡(x)=∫x∞exp⁡(−u)u​𝑑u.\displaystyle H(x)=\int_{x}^{\infty}\frac{\exp(-u)}{u}du. (43)

When ℂ​t>r2−ri2{\mathbb{C}}t>\sqrt{r^{2}-r_{i}^{2}}, the function fν~​(r,t)f_{\tilde{\nu}}(r,t) is defined as

fν~​(r,t)\displaystyle f_{\tilde{\nu}}(r,t) =\displaystyle= ri4​r{[1+rri−1ri​σν~]exp(−σν~(r−ri))\displaystyle\frac{r_{i}}{4r}\left\{\left[1+\frac{r}{r_{i}}-\frac{1}{r_{i}\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}}}\right]\exp\left(-\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}}(r-r_{i})\right)\right. (44)
