Notice that this is different from the commonly used solution under diffusion approximation [23], as the high frequency bins are actually optically thin.

To calculate the solution numerically, we take the Rosseland mean opacity for each frequency bin κa,f\kappa_{a,f} to be the monochromatic value shown in Figure 3 at frequency (ν~f+ν~f+1)/2(\tilde{\nu}_{f}+\tilde{\nu}_{f+1})/2. The numerical solution at radius r=0.04r=0.04 and time t=0.042/ℂt=0.042/{\mathbb{C}} is shown as red dots in the bottom panel of Figure 3. To get the monochromatic radiation energy density, we simply take Er,f/(ν~f+1−ν~f)E_{r,f}/(\tilde{\nu}_{f+1}-\tilde{\nu}_{f}). The numerical solution agrees very well with the analytical solution shown as the dashed line in the same figure. In the low frequency part (ν~<0.6\tilde{\nu}<0.6) where the domain is optically thick, the spectrum is dominated by local blackbody emission at temperature Tg=0.03T_{g}=0.03. For the high frequency part (ν~>0.6\tilde{\nu}>0.6), it is dominated by the attenuated emission from the inner boundary rir_{i}. Notice that for the first bin, Er,0E_{r,0} still agrees with the frequency integrated analytical solution for ν~∈[0,3×10−3]\tilde{\nu}\in[0,3\times 10^{-3}] very well. The estimated monochromatic radiation energy density in the first bin, which is not the quantity that we evolve, is slightly above the analytical value at ν~=1.5×10−3\tilde{\nu}=1.5\times 10^{-3} because we assume the spectrum is constant inside that bin.

IV.3 Tests of Frame Transformation

The frequency shift due to Doppler effect is handled by the Lorentz transformation as given by equation 4 for specific intensities between lab and co-moving frames. We first test that the transformation is satisfied numerically and then show that it can correctly capture the frequency dependence of opacity.

We set up a 1D periodic domain covering the region [0,1][0,1] with 16 grid points. We use 20 frequency groups and cover ν~∈[0.1,15]\tilde{\nu}\in[0.1,15] logarithmically. As a first step to just test the frame transformation, all the opacities are 0 so that there is no gas and radiation interaction. We simply measure the radiation quantities in the lab and co-moving frames respectively. For simplicity, we only use two angles in each cell and initialize the specific intensities with a blackbody spectrum in the lab frame at temperature T=1T=1. A uniform velocity v=0.134​cv=0.134c is applied to the gas. The system is already in steady state and the frame transformation does not cause any change of the solution numerically by design. Theoretically expected spectra for the specific intensities along two different directions are shown as black and red lines in Figure 4. The intensity with 𝒏⋅𝒗<0{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}<0 gets boosted while the intensity with 𝒏⋅𝒗>0{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}>0 is reduced in the co-moving frame according to equation 4. Since we only evolve the frequency integrated intensities in each bin, we can estimate the monochromatic values at the center of each frequency bin by I0,f/(νf+1−νf)I_{0,f}/(\nu_{f+1}-\nu_{f}). This can be done for the first 19 bins, which are shown as black and red squares in Figure 4. Our numerical solution I0,fI_{0,f} always match the theoretically expected frequency integrated values in each bin. Between ν~=0.1\tilde{\nu}=0.1 and ν~=15\tilde{\nu}=15 where the frequency space is resolved with 18 bins, the monochromatic intensities also agree with the analytical values. Our numerical estimate at ν~=0.05\tilde{\nu}=0.05 is always larger because the spectrum is assumed to be flat in each bin.

To test how the Lorentz transformation interacts with the source terms together, we use a frequency and spatial dependent absorption opacity defined in the co-moving frame as

κa,f=κp,f\displaystyle\kappa_{a,f}=\kappa_{p,f} =\displaystyle= 100​exp⁡[−[((ν~f+ν~f+1)/2−1)/0.3]2]\displaystyle 100\exp\left[-\left[((\tilde{\nu}_{f}+\tilde{\nu}_{f+1})/2-1)/0.3\right]^{2}\right] (45)
×\displaystyle\times exp⁡[−100​(x−0.5)2].\displaystyle\exp\left[-100\left(x-0.5\right)^{2}\right].

The opacity in the last frequency bin is set to 0. Example profiles of the opacity as a function of spatial location and frequency are shown in Figure 5. Scattering opacity is 0 in this test. Gas density and temperature are fixed to be 1 for the whole simulation domain in this test and they do not evolve. Gas velocity is 0 in the first step. Total optical depth across the box reaches a maximum value 15.715.7 in the frequency bin ν~∈[0.77,1.01)\tilde{\nu}\in[0.77,1.01) and then drops quickly for other bins. For ν~<0.34\tilde{\nu}<0.34 or ν~>1.33\tilde{\nu}>1.33, total optical depth across the box is smaller than 11. We still use two angles per cell for specific intensities in this test for simplicity and they are initialized to be 0. At the left boundary x=0x=0, the incoming specific intensities are set to a constant value 104​ar​T04/4​π10^{4}a_{r}T^{4}_{0}/4\pi for all frequency bins while outgoing specific intensities are set to 0. For the right boundary at x=1x=1, we copy the outgoing specific intensities from the last active zone to the ghost zones while set incoming specific intensities to be 0. The injected radiation field will propagate through the simulation domain and get attenuated around x=0.5x=0.5. We measure the steady state radiation energy densities in the lab frame as a function of frequencies at the right boundary, which are shown as the black lines labeled with v=0v=0 in Figure 6. The spectrum shape of Er,fE_{r,f} basically follows the frequency dependence of opacity κa\kappa_{a} as shown in Figure 5. For the two bins around ν~=1\tilde{\nu}=1 where the total optical depth is much larger than 1, Er,fE_{r,f} approaches the local emissivity ε0,f\varepsilon_{0,f}, which is taken to be blackbody emission with local gas temperature T=1T=1. For other bins, the reduction radiation energy density follows the expected attenuation exp⁡(−τf)\exp(-\tau_{f}), where τf\tau_{f} is the integrated optical depth across the whole simulation domain for each frequency bin.

We now keep everything the same but set the gas velocity to be v=0.05​cv=0.05c. Since co-moving frame frequencies are related to the lab frame frequencies via equation 2 and the opacity given in equation 45 is always applied in the co-moving frame, intensities with 𝒏⋅𝒗>0{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}>0 will shift the attenuation to a lightly higher frequency and intensities with 𝒏⋅𝒗<0{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}<0 will move to the opposite direction. Because Er,fE_{r,f} is dominated by the right propagating intensities, the spectrum of Er,fE_{r,f} is also shifted to higher frequencies as shown in the top panel of Figure 6. Similarly when gas has velocity v=−0.05​cv=-0.05c, the spectrum of Er,fE_{r,f} is shifted to lower frequencies as shown in the bottom panel of Figure 6. The results can be quantitatively checked with the mixed frame formula to the first order of v/cv/c [46]. If we neglect contribution from emissitivity, lab frame specific intensities are attenuated with lab frame monochromatic opacity κ⁡(ν)≈κ0​(ν)​[1−(𝒏⋅𝒗/c)​(1+∂log⁡κ0/∂log⁡ν)]\kappa(\nu)\approx\kappa_{0}(\nu)\left[1-\left({\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}/c\right)\left(1+\partial\log\kappa_{0}/\partial\log\nu\right)\right], where κ0​(ν)\kappa_{0}(\nu) is the opacity given by equation 45 but evaluated at the lab frame frequency ν\nu. This is derived using the relation κ⁡(ν)=γ⁡(1−𝒏⋅𝒗/c)​κ0​(ν0)\kappa(\nu)=\gamma\left(1-{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}/c\right)\kappa_{0}(\nu_{0}). We average κ⁡(ν)\kappa(\nu) for each frequency bin to get the lab frame κa,f\kappa_{a,f}, which is then used to calculate the new attenuation exp⁡(−τf)\exp(-\tau_{f}). This can explain the numerical solution very well except the bin ν~∈[0.6,1.3]\tilde{\nu}\in[0.6,1.3], where Er,fE_{r,f} is determined by local emissivity as it is optically thick and the above simple analysis does not apply.

IV.4 Tests of the Kompaneets Solver

In this section, we describe several tests of the Kompaneets solver implemented with our multi-group RT algorithm. Particularly, we will quantify the accuracy of the solver as a function of the number of frequency groups.

IV.4.1 Spectrum Evolution with A Delta function Initial Condition

If we neglect the stimulated emission term, Kompaneets equation becomes linear with respect to nν~n_{\tilde{\nu}} and it can be solved analytically. [5] gave an exact solution to describe the spectrum evolution at any time when the initial condition is the Green’s function at a particular frequency. In order to compare our numerical solutions to the analytical solutions, we set the stimulated emission term to be 0 in the solver while keeping everything else the same. Time evolution of the solution is typically described by the parameter y≡[c​ρ​κes​k​T/(me​c2)]​ty\equiv\left[c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}kT/(m_{e}c^{2})\right]t and all gas quantities are fixed in this test. We choose the parameters and unit system such that me​c2/k​T=100m_{e}c^{2}/kT=100 and c​ρ​κes=1000c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}=1000. The spatial and angular grids are not relevant for this test. We simply use a 1D domain from 0 to 1 with 32 grid points and two angles per cell. We use logarithmic frequency spacing to cover ν~∈[0.001,100]\tilde{\nu}\in[0.001,100] with Nf=100N_{f}=100. We limit the time step to be Δ​t=1.55×10−4\Delta t=1.55\times 10^{-4} so that the thermalization process can be properly resolved as it is equivalent to Δ​y=1.55×10−3\Delta y=1.55\times 10^{-3}. To mimic the delta function in the initial condition of the analytical solution, we initialize the frequency integrated specific intensities in the frequency bin ν~∈[0.91,1.02)\tilde{\nu}\in[0.91,1.02) to be 1 and 0 for all the others. The frequency dependent photon occupation number normalized by the number density of the initial delta function at frequency ν~0\tilde{\nu}_{0} for any yy parameter is (equation 33 of Becker 5)

nG\displaystyle n_{G} (ν~,ν~0,y)=32πe−9y/4ν~0−2ν~−2e(ν~0−ν~)/2\displaystyle(\tilde{\nu},\tilde{\nu}_{0},y)=\frac{32}{\pi}e^{-9y/4}\tilde{\nu}_{0}^{-2}\tilde{\nu}^{-2}e^{(\tilde{\nu}_{0}-\tilde{\nu})/2} (46)
×\displaystyle\times ∫0∞e−u2​y​u​sinh⁡(π​u)(1+4​u2)​(9+4​u2)​W2,i​u​(ν~0)​W2,i​u​(ν~)​𝑑u\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-u^{2}y}\frac{u\sinh(\pi u)}{(1+4u^{2})(9+4u^{2})}W_{2,iu}(\tilde{\nu}_{0})W_{2,iu}(\tilde{\nu})du
+\displaystyle+ e−ν~2+e−ν~−2​y2​(2−ν~)​(2−ν~0)ν~0​ν~,\displaystyle\frac{e^{-\tilde{\nu}}}{2}+\frac{e^{-\tilde{\nu}-2y}}{2}\frac{(2-\tilde{\nu})(2-\tilde{\nu}_{0})}{\tilde{\nu}_{0}\tilde{\nu}},

where W2,i​u​(ν~)W_{2,iu}(\tilde{\nu}) is the Whittaker function. This can be converted to the monochromatic radiation energy density Er​(ν~)E_{r}(\tilde{\nu}), which are shown as the solid lines in Figure 7 for different yy parameters with ν~0=1\tilde{\nu}_{0}=1. For the numerical solution, we calculate Er​(ν~)E_{r}(\tilde{\nu}) as Er,f/(ν~f+1−ν~f)E_{r,f}/(\tilde{\nu}_{f+1}-\tilde{\nu}_{f}), which are shown as open circles in the same figure. The numerical solution is more diffusive at the early time y≤0.1y\leq 0.1 but agrees with the analytical solution very well at the later time. The discrepancy at the earlier time is likely due to the fact that our initial condition is not a true delta function. This is also seen in other codes that performed similar test [49].

IV.4.2 Compton Thermalization

Compton can be the dominant thermalization process for low density, high temperature gas such as the corona region of accretion disks. To test the capability of our Kompaneets solver to evolve the gas temperature in this scattering dominated regime, we setup a 1D domain covering x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1] with 32 grid points and we use 2 angles per cell for specific intensities. Temperature unit is chosen to be T0=104T_{0}=10^{4} K and initial gas temperature is T=106T=10^{6} K. Uniform density ρ=10−10\rho=10^{-10} g/cm3 is adopted for the whole box. The opacity and time unit are chosen so that y=[c​ρ​κes​k​T/(me​c2)]​t=428.99​ty=\left[c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}kT/(m_{e}c^{2})\right]t=428.99t. We use Nf=150N_{f}=150 for the frequency grid and logarithmic spacing to cover ν~∈[0.01,500]\tilde{\nu}\in[0.01,500]. We initialize the radiation field with a blackbody spectrum at temperature T0T_{0} and let the system evolve to steady sate. Histories of gas temperature and effective radiation temperature Tr≡(∑f=0Nf−1Er,f/ar)1/4T_{r}\equiv(\sum_{f=0}^{N_{f}-1}E_{r,f}/a_{r})^{1/4} are shown in the top panel of Figure 8 and steady state spectrum is shown in the bottom panel of the same figure. The analytic solution can be calculated based on total energy conservation as well as the fact that total photon numbers remain the same for pure scattering. Photon occupation number in steady state should be nν~=1/[λ​exp⁡(ν~/T)−1]n_{\tilde{\nu}}=1/\left[\lambda\exp(\tilde{\nu}/T)-1\right], where the coefficient λ\lambda is constrained by the total photon numbers in the initial condition. With another constraint of total energy conservation, we can determine the gas temperature in steady state, which is T=70.46​T0T=70.46T_{0} and agrees with the numerical solution very well. This is also consistent with the Compton temperature as given by equation 20. If we do not solve the Kompaneets equation but assume photons have a black body spectrum, gas and radiation temperature needs to be the same in steady state, which will be Tb​d=4.03​T0T_{bd}=4.03T_{0} in this case. Clearly, gas temperature will be significantly underestimated.

In real multi-dimensional simulations, it can be too expensive to use 150150 frequency bins coupled with the angular grid. It is interesting to see how the results will depend on our resolution in frequency space. The steady state gas and radiation temperature as a function of total number of frequency bins NfN_{f} are shown in Figure 9. If only 55 frequency bins are used, we get T=52.4T=52.4. The error is reduced to 10%10\% when the frequency resolution is increased to 2020. The solution already reaches the accurate value with 5050 frequency bins. It is interesting to see that even solving the Kompaneets equation using 5 frequency bins, the solution we get is much better compared with the case if blackbody spectrum is assumed.

IV.4.3 Bulk Componization

Gas mechanical energy can also be exchanged with radiation energy directly via the forms of radiation work (for convergent and divergent flows) and radiation viscosity (for shear flows) terms. When the bulk velocity of electrons |𝒗||{\mbox{\boldmath$v$}}| is larger than 3​kB​T/me\sqrt{3k_{B}T/m_{e}} [59], Compton process by the bulk motions can be more important than Compton due to thermal motions of electrons. This can happen in strongly radiation pressure dominated flows around supermassive black holes, where bulk velocity of the flow or turbulent velocity can exceed thermal electron velocity [53, 79, 81, 70, 36, 37, 93]. In our multi-group algorithm developed here, scattering, absorption and emission are all calculated in the fluid rest frame. Bulk velocity of electrons relative to photons in different frequency group and different angular directions are taken care of by self-consistent Lorentz transformation.

To demonstrate how the bulk Compton effects are captured, we consider two simplified test problems for pure convergent/divergent flow and shear flow respectively. We first set up a 1D domain covering x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1] with 3232 grid points. Gas temperature is fixed to T0=105T_{0}=10^{5} K and the dimensionless speed of light ℂ=8193.11{\mathbb{C}}=8193.11. Density unit is chosen so that the dimensionless radiation pressure unit ℙ=1{\mathbb{P}}=1. Constant density and scattering opacity are used so that ρ​κes=10\rho\kappa_{\rm es}=10, which means total scattering optical depth is 10 across the whole box. Absorption opacity is 0. We use 16 angles to resolve the angular distribution of specific intensities and logarithmic frequency spacing to cover ν~∈[0.1,104]\tilde{\nu}\in[0.1,10^{4}] with Nf=40N_{f}=40. Periodic boundary condition is used for the radiation field while gas quantities are not evolved in this test. Isotropic specific intensities are initialized with blackbody spectrum at temperature T0T_{0}. We first set the flow velocity to 0 and let the system evolve. We do confirm that our Compton solver is able to maintain the blackbody spectrum. Then we fix the flow velocity to be vx=vm​sin⁡(2​π​x)v_{x}=v_{m}\sin(2\pi x) with the amplitude vm=300v_{m}=300, which corresponds to 8.93​kB​T0/me8.93\sqrt{k_{B}T_{0}/m_{e}}. As discussed by [36], if the photon mean free path is much longer or smaller than the length scale of velocity gradient, which is the box size in this test, pure convergent/divergent flows cannot change the photon spectrum. The parameters in this test are chosen so that photon diffusion speed is comparable to the advection speed so that the spectrum can be significantly modified by bulk Compton. At the beginning when velocity is added, the isotropic lab frame specific intensities will no longer be isotropic in the co-moving frame. Scattering will tend to isotropize the intensities in the co-moving frame while thermal Compton as well as velocity gradient shift the photons in the frequency space. Spatial radiation pressure gradient also develops because of the non-uniform velocity gradient. We calculate spatial variation of the radiation energy density for each frequency group as

δ​Er​(x,ν~)≡Er(x,ν~)−<Er(x,ν~)>x<Er(x,ν~)>x,\displaystyle\delta E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu})\equiv\frac{E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu})-<E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu})>_{x}}{<E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu})>_{x}}, (47)

where <Er(x,ν~)>x<E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu})>_{x} is the spatially averaged monochromatic radiation energy density at frequency ν~\tilde{\nu}. Spatial and frequency distribution of δ​Er​(x,ν~)\delta E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu}) at time t=2t=2, which corresponds to y=[c​ρ​κes​k​T0/(me​c2)]​t=2.76y=[c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}kT_{0}/(m_{e}c^{2})]t=2.76, is shown in Figure 10. Since bulk motions change photon energies at the rate proportional to the photon frequency [36], at low frequencies (ν~⪅1\tilde{\nu}\lessapprox 1), photon diffusion dominates and Er,ν~E_{r,\tilde{\nu}} is very uniform across the whole simulation box with |δ​Er​(x,ν~)||\delta E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu})| smaller than 10−310^{-3}. The small enhancement of Er​(x,ν~)E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu}) correlates with the velocity magnitude, which represents the difference between lab frame and co-moving frame radiation energy densities since (vx/c)2<1.3×10−3(v_{x}/c)^{2}<1.3\times 10^{-3}. At high frequencies (ν~>1\tilde{\nu}>1), δ​Er​(x,ν~)\delta E_{r}(x,\tilde{\nu}) then correlates with d​vx/d​xdv_{x}/dx very well. It peaks at the center where velocity converges and the minimum is at the edge where velocity diverges.

Even though the integrated d​vx/d​xdv_{x}/dx over the whole box is 0, total radiation energy density in the simulation domain still increases because radiation pressure at x=0.5x=0.5 is slightly larger than the radiation pressure at x=0x=0. Therefore the net radiation energy density increasing rate due to the radiation work term is also proportional to v2v^{2} in this test. The thermal Compton term then transfers energy from photons to gas as we fix the gas temperature to T=1T=1, which becomes smaller than the effective Compton temperature of photons. At time t=2t=2, total radiation energy density ErE_{r} integrated over the whole simulation domain and all the frequency groups reaches 15​ar​T0415a_{r}T_{0}^{4} and spectrum of the box integrated Er​(ν~)E_{r}(\tilde{\nu}) is shown as the red line in Figure 11. The peak has moved to higher frequencies compared with the initial blackbody spectrum. Since we only have scattering in this test and the simulation domain is periodic, we can compare the spectrum to the Bose-Einstein distribution n⁡(ν~)=1/[λ​exp⁡(ν~/Teff)−1]n(\tilde{\nu})=1/[\lambda\exp(\tilde{\nu}/T_{\text{eff}})-1], where the effective temperature can be estimated as Teff=T+me​vm2/(3​kB)=27.57​TT_{\text{eff}}=T+m_{e}v_{m}^{2}/(3k_{B})=27.57T [59, 36] and λ\lambda is related to the chemical potential of the distribution. We then fix the parameter λ\lambda by requiring that the total radiation energy density from this distribution is the same as ErE_{r}. The spectrum is shown as the dashed green line in Figure 11, which matches the peak of the numerical solution very well. But spectrum of the numerical solution is slightly flatter in both the low and high frequency parts, which is likely because this is a mixture of photons from different locations of the box with different local spectra as shown in Figure 10.

We then consider a shear flow in the 2D domain (x,y)∈[0,1]×[0,1](x,y)\in[0,1]\times[0,1] as vy=vm​sin⁡(2​π​x)v_{y}=v_{m}\sin(2\pi x) with vm=300v_{m}=300 and the horizontal velocity is 0. We use 32×3232\times 32 grid points for the spatial resolution and 40 angles for the angular resolution. All the other quantities are the same as in the last test. Radiation energy density is increased everywhere initially via the radiation viscosity term. Then the thermal Compton term transfers energy from photons to the gas. The energy increasing rate in this case is typically small because the off-diagonal components of radiation pressure is small compared with the diagonal components and only the velocity shear rate across the photon mean free path can contribute. Spectrum of spatially averaged radiation energy density at time t=2t=2 is shown in Figure 12. Total radiation energy density ErE_{r} is only increased to 2.15​ar​T042.15a_{r}T_{0}^{4} at this time, which is 14%14\% of ErE_{r} in the last case at the corresponding time. We estimate the effective temperature of photons resulting from this shear flow using equation 39 of [36] as Teff=T+f⁡(τk)​me​⟨v2⟩/(3​kB)=1.99​TT_{\text{eff}}=T+f(\tau_{k})m_{e}\langle v^{2}\rangle/(3k_{B})=1.99T, where the mean velocity square is ⟨v2⟩=vm2/2\langle v^{2}\rangle=v_{m}^{2}/2 and the optical depth reduction factor is fτk=0.074f_{\tau_{k}}=0.074 for τk=10/(2​π)\tau_{k}=10/(2\pi). A spectrum of Bose-Einstein distribution at the effective temperature TeffT_{\text{eff}} is shown as the dashed green line in Figure 12. The Bose-Einstein distribution is also normalized to match ErE_{r} in the numerical solution. It can explain the peak and low frequency end of the calculated spectrum very well. However, the numerical solution shows a much more extended high frequency tail, which cannot be captured by this Bose-Einstein distribution.

IV.4.4 Compton Scattering in a Stratified Atmosphere

To check how the Kompaneets solver is coupled to other terms in the RT equation, we set up a 1D domain covering x∈[0,3​L0]x\in[0,3L_{0}] using 128 grid points with the density profile ρ⁡(x)=ρ0​exp⁡(−x2)\rho(x)=\rho_{0}\exp(-x^{2}). Here the length unit is L0=3×1014L_{0}=3\times 10^{14} cm and ρ0=10−10\rho_{0}=10^{-10} g/cm3. We vary the scattering opacity κes\kappa_{\rm es} so that total optical depth τ=∫03​L0κes​ρ​𝑑x\tau=\int_{0}^{3L_{0}}\kappa_{\rm es}\rho dx reaches the desired value. Absorption opacity is 0 in this test. Gas temperature is set to a constant value T=106T=10^{6} K. We inject photons from the bottom at x=0x=0 with a 10410^{4} K black body spectrum isotropically. At the top boundary x=3​L0x=3L_{0}, we copy the outgoing specific intensities from the last active zone to the ghost zones and set the incoming specific intensities to be 0. We only use two angles per cell (the two-stream approximation) so that we can check the numerical solution easily. All the hydro variables are held fixed in this test. We use 100100 frequency bins and logarithmic frequency grid to cover ν~∈[0.1,500]\tilde{\nu}\in[0.1,500]. We collect photons at the surface x=3​L0x=3L_{0} to determine its spectra when we vary the total optical depth τ\tau from 300 to 10, which are shown in Figure 13. All terms in the Kompaneets equation are included in this test. The typical diffusion time from the bottom to top is t=3​L0​τ/ct=3L_{0}\tau/c. Then the Compton yy parameter is given by y=[c​ρ​κes​kB​T/(me​c2)]​3​L0​τ/c≈5×10−4​τ2y=\left[c\rho\kappa_{\rm es}k_{B}T/(m_{e}c^{2})\right]3L_{0}\tau/c\approx 5\times 10^{-4}\tau^{2}. When τ=30\tau=30 and 1010, y≪1y\ll 1 and the change of radiation spectra due to Compton scattering is minimal. Spectra of the emitting photons are close to the black body spectrum we injected from the base. For τ=100\tau=100, the spectrum is significantly modified by Compton scattering. While the whole domain has τ=300\tau=300 and y≫1y\gg 1, the spectrum is saturated to the gas temperature T=106T=10^{6} K. To check the numerical solution, we discretize the steady state transport equation 23 and the Kompaneets equation in both frequency and spatial grids. We confirm that they are indeed satisfied by the numerical solution.

IV.5 Shadow Test with Two Frequency Groups

One application of the multi-group RT is that it can handle radiation coming from different sources, which may have quite different characteristic frequencies and associated opacities. As a prove of principle, we extend the classical shadow test to two frequency groups, which cover the frequency range ν~∈[0,5)\tilde{\nu}\in[0,5) and ν~∈[5,∞)\tilde{\nu}\in[5,\infty) respectively. We use a 2D simulation domain (x,y)∈[−0.5,0.5]×[−0.3,0.3](x,y)\in[-0.5,0.5]\times[-0.3,0.3] with 512×256512\times 256 grid points. Each cell has 40 angles for specific intensities in this test. Temperature unit T0T_{0} is chosen so that the dimensionless speed of light is ℂ=1.9×105{\mathbb{C}}=1.9\times 10^{5}. Density has the shape ρ⁡(x,y)=1+9/{1+exp⁡[10​[(x/0.1)2+(y/0.06)2−1]]}\rho(x,y)=1+9/\left\{1+\exp[10\left[(x/0.1)^{2}+(y/0.06)^{2}-1\right]]\right\} and temperature is set to be T⁡(x,y)=1/ρ⁡(x,y)T(x,y)=1/\rho(x,y), which varies from 0.10.1 inside the cloud to 11 outside the cloud. Gas velocity is 0 and all gas quantities are fixed in this test. The first frequency group represents low energy photons emitted by the gas and it has absorption opacity κa,0=κp,0=ρ​T−3.5\kappa_{a,0}=\kappa_{p,0}=\rho T^{-3.5}. Scattering opacity is 0 for this group. At the left and right boundaries, incoming specific intensities are set to be 0 while outgoing ones are copied from the last active zone to the ghost zones. The second frequency group represents high energy photons emitted by external sources. At the left boundary, incoming intensities with angle 18∘18^{\circ} relative to the xx axis are set to ar​Ti4/(8​π​wn)a_{r}T_{i}^{4}/(8\pi w_{n}) while all the other rays are set to be 0, where Ti=6T_{i}=6 and wnw_{n} is the angular quadrature weight for each ray. This is designed so that the mean radiation energy density for this group injected from the left boundary is Er,1=4​π​∑nIf​(n)​wn=ar​Ti4E_{r,1}=4\pi\sum_{n}I_{f}(n)w_{n}=a_{r}T_{i}^{4}. At the right boundary, the same boundary condition as used for the first group is adopted. The top and bottom boundaries are periodic for both frequency groups. The second group is set to have a constant absorption opacity κa,1=κp,1=1\kappa_{a,1}=\kappa_{p,1}=1 and scattering opacity is also 0. Radiation energy densities in the two frequency groups after the system reaches steady state are shown in Figure 14. For the first group, Er,0/ar​T04E_{r,0}/a_{r}T_{0}^{4} is very close to (T/T0)4(T/T_{0})^{4}, which varies from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Total optical depth across the cloud in the second frequency group is only 2.82.8. Therefore, photons in this group penetrate the cloud while get attenuated. Umbra and penumbra are clearly captured in this frequency group, although size of the umbra is reduced due to lower optical depth compared with similar test done for the grey case [32]. This will also result in different dynamics of the cloud if we let gas evolve with radiation field together [57], which will be studied in the future with more realistic conditions.

IV.6 Bondi Accretion with Compton Scattering

To demonstrate that the algorithm described here is able to handle the full radiation hydrodynamics with Compton scattering together, we set up a spherically symmetric one dimensional (1D) Bondi accretion flow and see how the solution will evolve with the full radiation hydrodynamics turned on. We do not include magnetic field here as it does not make any difference in 1D. There is no analytical solution to compare with in this case. Instead, this is commonly used as a proof of principle calculation for radiation MHD codes [17] as well as tests for Compton scattering [79, 59, 58, 81].

We initialize the simulation with the classical Bondi solution [6, 18] with an effective adiabatic index γB=1.4\gamma_{B}=1.4. We consider accretion onto a black hole with mass MBH=106​M⊙M_{\rm{BH}}=10^{6}M_{\odot}, where M⊙M_{\odot} is the solar mass. Adiabatic sound speed and density at infinity are chosen to be c∞=4.33×107​cm/sc_{\infty}=4.33\times 10^{7}\ \text{cm/s} and ρ∞=10−17​g/cm3\rho_{\infty}=10^{-17}\ \text{g/cm}^{3}. Mass accretion rate of the Bondi solution is then M˙B=π​rB2​ρ∞​c∞​(2/(5−3​γB))(5−3​γB)/(2​(γB−1))\dot{M}_{B}=\pi r_{B}^{2}\rho_{\infty}c_{\infty}\left(2/(5-3\gamma_{B})\right)^{\left(5-3\gamma_{B}\right)/\left(2\left(\gamma_{B}-1\right)\right)}, where Bondi radius rBr_{B} is defined as rB=G​MBH/c∞2r_{B}=GM_{\rm{BH}}/c_{\infty}^{2} and GG is the gravitational constant. This is about 1212 times the Eddington accretion rate for the parameters we choose. Since rBr_{B} is 4.8×1054.8\times 10^{5} times the gravitational radius, we cannot cover the whole radial range from the gravitational radius to rBr_{B}. Instead we focus on the outer region near rBr_{B} to see how the solution will be modified with RT turned on. This will also cover the photosphere, which is not the case if only the free fall part in the Bondi solution is considered [79, 17]. We use 1D spherical polar coordinate covering radial range r/rB∈[10−3,1]r/r_{B}\in[10^{-3},1] with 512 grid points logarithmically. In the frequency space, we use logarithmic grid to cover ν~∈[10−3,102]\tilde{\nu}\in[10^{-3},10^{2}] with Nf=50N_{f}=50. We set density and pressure in the inner ghost zones so that their gradients are continuous across the inner boundary. Radial velocity in the inner ghost zones is set by requiring the mass flux to be continuous after density is determined in the boundary. The same boundary condition is also applied to the fluid variables at the outer boundary. For specific intensities at both inner and outer boundaries, we require I​r2Ir^{2} to be continuous across the boundary for all angles and frequency groups. To initialize the simulation, we first calculate the radial profiles of the classical Bondi solution based on the fact that mass accretion rate and the Bernoulli parameter vr2/2+γB​cs2/(γB−1)−G​MBH/rv_{r}^{2}/2+\gamma_{B}c_{s}^{2}/\left(\gamma_{B}-1\right)-GM_{\rm{BH}}/r are constant [18]. Here cs2c_{s}^{2} is the ratio between total pressure and density. We then require that radiation and gas are in thermal equilibrium with the total pressure unchanged so that Pg+Pr=ρ​cs2P_{g}+P_{r}=\rho c_{s}^{2}. Radiation pressure is larger than gas pressure by a factor of 6.8×103−1046.8\times 10^{3}-10^{4} but gas temperature only varies from 0.02​T00.02T_{0} to 0.44​T00.44T_{0}, where T0=105T_{0}=10^{5} K is the fiducial unit for temperature. The fiducial density and velocity units are chosen to be ρ0=10−10​g/cm3,v0=3.66×106​cm/s\rho_{0}=10^{-10}\ \text{g/cm}^{3},v_{0}=3.66\times 10^{6}\text{cm/s} so that the dimensionless parameters ℙ=565.2{\mathbb{P}}=565.2 and ℂ=8193.1{\mathbb{C}}=8193.1 for this test problem. We take the electron scattering opacity to be 0.34​cm2/g0.34\ \text{cm}^{2}/\text{g} and frequency dependent absorption opacity as 3.68×1056Ta−1/2ρν−3cm2/g3.68\times 10^{56}T_{a}^{-1/2}\rho\nu^{-3}\text{cm}^{2}/\text{g}, where the temperature parameter is Ta≡max​(T,0.1​T0)T_{a}\equiv\text{max}(T,0.1T_{0}). For each frequency group, we simply take the frequency value at the center of each bin to calculate the absorption opacity.

Radial profiles of various quantities for the initial condition as well as steady state solution are shown in Figure 15. Density and radial velocity increase slightly to make the accretion rate increased by a factor of 3. However, gas temperature has dropped by a factor of 5−505-50 from the inner to outer regions, which makes the whole simulation domain become supersonic. Radiation pressure is only 3030 times the gas pressure. This implies that the sonic point will be located at a much larger radius than what the original Bondi solution suggests. For the 1D accretion flow, the only dissipation mechanism is due to compression, which is very inefficient. For the radial range we have covered here, radiative luminosity in steady state is only 6.1×10−56.1\times 10^{-5} of the Eddington luminosity.

The calculation also provides spectra of the radiation field directly, which are shown in Figure 16 for three representative locations. We have normalized the radiation energy density in each frequency group by the frequency integrated radiation energy density at each radius so that we can compare their spectrum shape in the same plot. Total optical depth for scattering opacity across the simulation domain is 2020 for all frequency groups, while integrated optical depth for absorption varies from 10510^{5} at the low frequency end to 10−910^{-9} at the high frequency group. Optical depth for the effective absorption, which is defined as the geometric mean of absorption and total opacity, is smaller than 1 for frequency groups with ν~>0.28\tilde{\nu}>0.28. Near the inner region at 0.0012​rB0.0012r_{B}, spectrum in the low frequency range (ν~≲0.5\tilde{\nu}\lesssim 0.5) follows the blackbody shape very well. For high frequencies (ν~≳0.5\tilde{\nu}\gtrsim 0.5) where effective absorption optical depth is smaller than 1, the spectrum follows a power law shape ν~−2.4\tilde{\nu}^{-2.4} very well. In fact, the high frequency tails of spectra at all three radii follow the same power law shape, which is likely produced by bulk Comptonization due to the convergent flow. The inflow velocity is larger than 3​kB​T/me\sqrt{3k_{B}T/m_{e}} by a factor of 1010 to 3030 in the whole simulation domain and gas temperature is too small to produce any thermal Compton effect. Since radial velocity ends up reaching the free fall limit in the whole simulation domain, if only first order v/cv/c effect is considered, the high frequency spectrum will have a universal power law shape ν~−2\tilde{\nu}^{-2} [53]. When all the terms are considered properly, the power law slope will depend on detailed properties of the flow, which can vary between −2-2 and −3-3 for the accretion rate we are considering here according to the model studied by [81]. This is very consistent with the power law slope we get. At larger radii, more frequency groups become optically thin for effective absorption and scattering optical depth is also reduced, while parts of the spectra at the lowest frequency end still follow the blackbody shape. Spectrum peaks move to lower frequencies due to smaller gas temperature. If we treat bulk Compton scattering as thermal Compton with effective temperature Teff=me​vr2/(3​kB)T_{\text{eff}}=m_{e}v_{r}^{2}/(3k_{B}) [36], we can estimate the Compton yy parameter as y=τ2​(vr/c)2y=\tau^{2}\left(v_{r}/c\right)^{2}, which is 1 at r/rB=0.0013r/r_{B}=0.0013. This explains why the peak regions of the spectra become flatter at r/rB=0.01r/r_{B}=0.01 and r/rB=0.2r/r_{B}=0.2 similar to the spectra shown in Figure 13 (the red line).

V Discussion

The multi-group RT algorithm we have developed here is fully implicit for both the spatial transport term and the source terms. This is designed to work efficiently for a wide range of problems, particularly when the typical flow speed, sound speed or Alfvén velocity is much smaller than the speed of light. Therefore, time step of the whole radiation MHD scheme is not limited by the speed of light. The number of iterations we need for convergence in the implicit scheme is typically much smaller than the ratio between speed of light and the largest signal speed given by the MHD equations for all the test problems we have done. However, for systems with a flow speed comparable to the speed of light, it will be more efficient to solve the spatial transport term explicitly while still solve the source terms implicitly [35]. This can happen for either relativistic flows around compact objects, or non-relativistic systems with signal speed larger than ≳0.1​c\gtrsim 0.1c. In this way, time step will be limited by the CFL condition as defined by the speed of light but no iteration over the whole simulation domain is needed, as the implicit update for the source terms is completely local for each cell. This will also improve the parallel efficiency of the whole algorithm. It is very straightforward to convert the algorithm developed here to that case as we just need to change the term Δ​t​c​𝒏⋅∇Ifm+1\Delta tc{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{f}^{m+1} in equation 24 to Δ​t​c​𝒏⋅∇Ifm\Delta tc{\mbox{\boldmath$n$}}\cdot{\mbox{\boldmath$\nabla$}}I_{f}^{m}. The way we solve all the other terms are unchanged.

Performance of the overall multi-group radiation MHD algorithm will strongly depend on the number of iterations it takes to converge, which can vary significantly for different applications. The cost for each iteration is linearly proportional to N×NfN\times N_{f}. Coupling between different frequency groups in the source terms causes a few extra fourth order polynomial solvers (see section III.2) compared with the grey case. However, this additional cost is a negligible fraction of the overall cost. As a reference of performance for real applications that have used the code developed by [32], the simulations described in [21] adopt 120 angles per cell with 1283128^{3} spatial resolution and it takes about 1010 iterations to achieve a relative accuracy of 10−610^{-6} per time step. The code can update 10410^{4} cells per second per core using more than 4545 skylake nodes with 4040 cores per node. To update 10710^{7} cycles, which are typically needed to cover a few thermal time scales, it will cost about 10610^{6} core hours. Adding ≈10\approx 10 frequency groups will likely increase the cost by an order of magnitude unless a fewer number of angles can be used.

The scheme can also be used to calculate broad band spectrum when gas properties are given. For example, we can post process the simulation data generated by MHD simulations. For this purpose, we simply do not add radiation energy and momentum source terms back to the MHD equations. Even though the algorithm solves the full time dependent RT equation, we can evolve the system to reach steady state to get the broadband spectrum of the flow. This behaves like a relaxation method for time independent RT equation as normally assumed for spectrum calculations. However, future development is needed to speed up the convergence and the rate to reach steady state for this purpose.

The current algorithm will need a lot of frequency groups to follow the Doppler shift of each individual line in order to model line transport in principle, which is not affordable in real applications. We also assume the frequency grid is the same at different spatial locations for simplicity. This is not optimal when features in the frequency space shift with space. This can happen when temperature varies significantly with space, or Doppler effect causes systematic shift of frequencies. Adaptive frequency grid can be used in this case, which means we can use different frequency grids at different spatial locations. This is also necessary to model the line transport efficiently. It will require mapping specific intensities in different frequency grids at the boundary of each cell, which will be developed in future work.

Solvers for frequency and angular resolved RT calculations coupled with MHD simulations have been implemented in various codes to model stellar atmosphere and convection. The STAGGER code [52, 73] uses the Feautrier’s scheme to solve the RT equation along several inclined rays (one vertical, eight inclined) while MURaM [86] and CO5BOLD [19] adopt the short characteristic approach. All these codes bin the monochromatic opacities into several groups according to the height at which they mainly contribute to the radiative heating rate[51, 85]. The opacity groups may not be continuous in the frequency space. Our algorithm differs from these codes in many ways. They all neglect the time dependence as well as velocity dependence of specific intensities, which will significantly complicate any kind of opacity binning scheme. Radiation field is used to determine the heating and cooling rate of gas while momentum exchange between photons and gas is not considered in these codes. Simulations using these codes are typically done in Cartesian coordinate as short characteristic approach is not easy to implement in general curvilinear coordinate systems.

The algorithm developed here opens up new opportunities for a wide range of applications. Just to mention a few examples here, it can be used to improve radiation MHD simulations of black hole accretion disks [33] with a much better solver for Compton scattering in the corona region. It will also directly produce broad band spectra without the need of post processing. The scheme is also able to capture the collapse of hot accretion flows from optically thin to optically thick regimes due to Compton cooling much more efficiently compared with Monte Carlo method [13]. Interactions between supernova shocks and circumstellar material [42] can also be simulated accurately with this scheme. More importantly, the algorithm can be used to quantify whether grey approximation is appropriate or not, which is barely demonstrated before. When the dominant opacity depends on frequency, the algorithm can be used to test the accuracy of commonly adopted Planck mean and Rosseland mean opacities for thermal and momentum couplings between radiation and gas. A simple example is free-free opacity, which varies with frequency as ν−3[1−exp(−hν/kBT)]\nu^{-3}\left[1-\exp(-h\nu/k_{B}T)\right] for a given density and temperature and it is very relevant in many astrophysical systems [63]. It can be easily shown that the Rosseland mean value is smaller than the Planck mean value by a factor of ≈30\approx 30. The actual opacity that determines the radiation force for a given luminosity will depend on the full radiation spectrum and it is likely between the Rosseland mean and Planck mean values. Rosseland mean opacity only applies when it is optically thick for the whole frequency range and radiation and gas are in thermal equilibrium. Similar conclusion has been found for Wolf-Rayet stars where the Rosseland mean opacity significantly underestimates the flux weighted value based on frequency dependent RT calculations [64]. We can resolve the frequency dependence of free-free opacity very well using 1010 to 2020 frequency groups that covers ≈0.1​h​ν/kB​T\approx 0.1h\nu/k_{B}T to ≈10​h​ν/kB​T\approx 10h\nu/k_{B}T logarithmically, in which case the Rosseland and Planck mean values defined in each group will be very close to each other. The algorithm developed here will also be more accurate than many other multi-group approaches that adopt diffusion like approximations since we also resolve the full angular dependence of the radiation field. The region where grey approximation fails is also likely the place where diffusion approximation cannot apply.
